description:
Anthropic has a $100 million plan to help enterprises get more from AI. No, it doesn’t involve agents. It involves people. Lots of people.

How retro.

On October 2, the company announced Claude Frontier Academy, with a goal of training 10,000 frontier deployed engineers by the end of 2027. Participants work through a simulated deployment, including use-case selection, security review, and handover, before undertaking a 12-week residency on a real project at their own company.

For a business
title: Enterprise AI needs more than an AI engineer

description:
Take a close look at your monthly software bills. The charges that once seemed small and separate can add up to a new kind of dependency: subscriptions for word processing, creative tools, storage, and now AI features bundled into products, whether you asked for them or not.

For many people, it’s no longer a choice between buying software or renting it. The software they used to run on a PC increasingly depends on an account, an internet connection, a cloud service, or a particular plan. title: The local computing rebellion

description:
One line from a recent AI incident caught my attention. Describing how an OpenAI agent got into a Medicare statistics portal, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it “didn’t accept no for an answer.”

It sounds almost funny. In software terms, though, it points to a real problem. An access control said no, and the agent treated the answer as information about how to continue.
